title: From “Bowling Alone” to scrolling alone
gist: On the Slow Boring podcast, Yglesias argues Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' predictions about declining churchgoing and the internet's failure to replace in-person community have held up decades later, while co-host Jerusalem pushes back on Putnam's causal claims and flags television's underexplored role in the book's own social-capital story.

insights.claim: Robert Putnam's 'Bowling Alone' forecasts of an imminent collapse of American churchgoing and his skepticism that the internet could substitute for in-person social interaction have both been vindicated in retrospect, according to Yglesias.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A once-controversial thesis about community decline is being reassessed as prescient decades on, relevant to anyone modeling long-run trends in religious affiliation and digital-versus-physical socializing.
insights.quote: controversial-at-the-time forecasts about things like an imminent collapse of American churchgoing and skepticism that the internet would provide a viable alternative to the social role of in-person interaction have been vindicated.
insights.locator: With that vantage point, I was genuinely surprised

insights.claim: Rereading 'Bowling Alone' as an adult, Yglesias was surprised how few pages are devoted to the book's central bowling-league metaphor and how well he thinks Putnam's broader argument holds up.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: A firsthand reread from someone present at the book's original cultural moment (as a student at Putnam's own college) lends credibility to the reassessment.
insights.quote: I was genuinely surprised by how few pages are occupied by the central metaphor about bowling and by how well I think Putnam’s arguments hold up in retrospect.

insights.claim: Co-host Jerusalem is less impressed with 'Bowling Alone,' arguing the causal chains Putnam draws between his preferred kinds of civic organizations and good social outcomes are convoluted and unclear.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Flags a specific empirical weak point in Putnam's thesis worth scrutinizing before treating 'more civic organizations' as a straightforward policy fix for social decline.
insights.quote: the causal chains linking Putnam’s preferred kinds of organizations to good outcomes are a bit convoluted and unclear.
insights.locator: She points out that the causal chains

insights.claim: Jerusalem frames Putnam's broader thesis as part of a 21st-century intellectual backlash against liberalism and individualism that she believes is having harmful effects in the present day.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Situates 'Bowling Alone'-style communitarianism within a live ideological debate about individualism versus collective obligation that still shapes current political discourse.
insights.locator: she situates his broad argument as part of a 21st-century backlash

insights.claim: By Putnam's own accounting in 'Bowling Alone,' roughly half of the decline in American social capital is attributable to people watching more and more television over time, which crowded out other kinds of civic and social activity.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Reframes today's debates over phones and social media as a repeat of a screen-driven social-capital dynamic Putnam already identified with television decades earlier.
insights.quote: roughly half the decline in social capital is caused by people watching more and more television over time and thus crowding out all other kinds of activities

insights.claim: Yglesias and Jerusalem agree there is a mismatch in 'Bowling Alone' between how few pages discuss television and how central a causal role Putnam assigns it, and that none of Putnam's proposed remedies directly address television's role.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Points to an actionable gap in a canonical social-capital text: if TV/screens are half the story, solutions that ignore screen time can't fully address the decline.
insights.quote: none of his proposed solutions confront it directly.
insights.locator: But he doesn’t spend that many pages on this point

insights.claim: Jerusalem raises the alternative hypothesis that it may be the content of video and streaming media itself — not merely the resulting loss of social capital — that generates the bad social outcomes commonly attributed to community decline.
insights.speaker: Matthew Yglesias
insights.so_what: Offers a competing causal mechanism (content effects vs. displacement effects) that matters for whether the fix is 'watch less' or 'watch different things.'
insights.quote: Jerusalem also raises the possibility that it may be the video content itself that generates bad outcomes rather than the decline in social capital.
